Gi9qrR-f83308-d1e4531.summary: Closing transitional note deferring further discussion of the velocity and temporal conditions of separated substances' motion to Book 2, followed by the reply to the first objection of the second dubitatio (that the soul's motion in departure can be instantaneous, though not necessarily so, and that this is not owing to any difference in power between soul and angel but to the fact that the relevant mutation [under the case considered] is the terminus of a motion, which cannot be said of angelic mutations in the same way) and the reply to the second objection (that, since the corruption of the body is not fully in act except at the terminus of the motion of corrupting, being in potency throughout the process, it is not proper to posit two actual termini or a last instant of the soul's being the body's form — motion, per Physics 3, being the act of a being in potency as such, while the terminus of motion, mutatum/corruptum esse, is where separation of soul from body actually occurs — hence such motion is not necessarily in time).
claims: The soul's motion of departure can (but need not) be instantaneous, not because of any deficiency of power relative to the angel, but because the relevant mutation, in the case considered, is the terminus of a (corruption) motion, unlike the angel's transition.

Since corruption is only fully actual at the terminus of the corrupting process (being merely in potency throughout, per the Physics 3 definition of motion), it is improper to posit a last actual instant of the soul's being form; hence this motion need not be temporal.
concepts: motion as act of a being in potency qua potency (Physics 3)
actuality only at the terminus of corruption

Gi9qrR-f83308-d1e4601.summary: Final reply, to the sed-contra objection (that corruption, being a mutation and terminus of motion, is necessarily instantaneous, hence so is the soul's departure): grants that corruption is necessarily instantaneous when taken precisely as the mutation/terminus of motion, and that, since bodily corruption is not the soul's separation from the body in every respect but only insofar as the body is its form, it follows validly that the soul necessarily ceases to be the body's form in an instant — but this does not entail that the soul is necessarily moved (i.e., departs) in that same instant, since after ceasing to be form it could remain in the body as a mover or by application of virtue. The proper resolution is thus the one already given in the principal solution: in the soul's departure, if it does cross the medium, its motion can be instantaneous or not, as has been shown.
claims: Corruption is necessarily instantaneous as the terminus of the corrupting motion, and hence the soul necessarily ceases to be the body's substantial form in an instant.
This does not entail that the soul is necessarily moved (departs) in that same instant, since it could remain present as mover or by application of virtue.
The definitive answer is that the soul's motion of departure can be instantaneous or not, as already established.

Gi9qrR-f83308-Dd1e142.summary: Article 1 (Utrum Angelus moveatur?) argues that motion belongs to angels not merely metaphorically but, in a qualified sense, properly. Five objections deny angelic motion on grounds drawn from Aristotelian physics and metaphysics (dependence of motion on matter; the metaphysician's vs. physicist's object; the impossibility of an impartible thing being partly in each terminus; the failure of angelic 'motion' to fit any recognized species of motion; and a per se/per accidens dilemma threatening to entail that God too moves). Patristic sed-contra authorities (Bede, Ambrose, Damascene) affirm angelic motion. The determinatio distinguishes two senses of motion in angels: a metaphorical sense, in which the angel's operation itself is called 'motion' (elaborated via Dionysius's threefold rectilinear/circular/oblique pattern, applied first to God and then to angels as a figure for reception and transmission of illumination), and a properly (though qualifiedly) intended sense, grounded in succession — not in the angel's being or natural power, which are immutable, but in its operations (both immanent acts of understanding/willing and transitive acts on external bodies), which is why such motion is more properly called motion 'through time' than 'through place.' The replies to the objections show, respectively, that angels possess an admixed potentiality (yliachin) sufficient for a genuine mode of motion; that the 'unmoved mover' argument applies only to motion as considered by natural philosophy (ordered to celestial bodies); that operating in a quantified place suffices for an impartible angel's motion, and that 'motion' is said equivocally of bodies and spirits so angelic motion need not fall under Aristotle's bodily species (though it bears analogical likeness to alteration and local motion); and that the angel is moved per se by virtue of operating in a quantified place and per accidens by an assumed body's motion, whereas God, being uncircumscribable, is moved in neither way.
claims: Motion belongs to angels not merely metaphorically but in a qualified, properly intended sense.
Angelic motion in the proper sense consists in succession among the angel's operations (immanent and transitive), not in any change of essence or natural power.

Angelic motion does not fall under Aristotle's bodily species of motion, since 'motion' is said equivocally of bodies and spirits, though angelic motion bears real analogical likeness to alteration and to local motion.
The angel moves per se (by operating in a quantified place) and per accidens (via an assumed body); God, being incircumscribable, is moved in neither sense.
concepts: equivocity of 'motion' across bodies and spirits

Gi9qrR-f83308-Dd1e1021.summary: Article 2 (Utrum Angelus, cum movetur, de necessitate transeat per medium?) concludes, against a conciliatory view that lets the angel skip the intervening medium at will, that an angel moving between two places must pass through the medium, on account of the order and connection of the parts of the universe. Two objections deny this on grounds of the angel's impartibility (which cannot be commensurated to a partible medium) and its mode of presence-by-operation (allowing it, like a thinking intellect, to skip intermediate places), reinforced by a mathematical worry that traversing a continuum's infinitely many points is impossible. Sed-contra arguments from Damascene and Aristotelian mutation-theory insist that anything now somewhere it was not before must have changed via the medium. The determinatio reframes local motion generally as a succession of a thing's being-in-place — by commensuration for bodies, by operation for spirits — and argues that although the angel's nature considered absolutely does not require place, the angel as a part of the ordered, interconnected universe is always determinately related (near/far) to other places, and therefore cannot skip from extreme to extreme without the medium. The replies clarify that traversing the medium requires only application of virtue, not commensuration; that in the narrow sense of 'operation' (producing transmutation) the angel need not affect the intervening medium, but in the broader sense (mere application of virtue) it always does, as required by cosmic order rather than local need; that the angel's practical (though not speculative) relation to the universe's parts must respect their real order; and that the infinite-points worry rests on falsely imagining angelic presence as commensuration, when in fact it is by operation on a quantified place, and intermediate points are merely potential, not actual, infinities.
claims: An angel moving between two places necessarily passes through the intervening medium, on account of the order and connection of the parts of the universe, even though its nature absolutely considered does not require place.
Traversing the medium requires only application of virtue to it, not commensuration to it as bodies are commensurated to place.
The angel's practical (operative) relation to the universe's ordered parts must respect their real spatial order, even though its speculative (intellectual) relation to them need not.

Gi9qrR-f83308-Dd1e1654.summary: Article 3 (Utrum Angelus, cum movetur, mutetur in tempore vel in instanti?), the longest and most technical article, concludes that angelic motion is always in time, whether the angel moves by application of virtue to diverse spaces or in an assumed body — though the 'time' in question is, in the case of application of virtue, a distinct, non-continuous kind of time (a bare succession of instants) rather than the continuous time that is the passio of the first (celestial) motion. Initial objections argue for instantaneous angelic motion on the grounds that only medial resistance (absent for an incorporeal mover) requires time, illustrated by the instantaneous multiplication of light, and by a proportionality argument threatening absurd equalities between bodily and angelic motion. Sed-contra arguments insist that per se, motion (if it is truly motion) must occur in time, and that admitting an 'instantaneous motion' would violate the principle that ever-faster motions can always be found. A lengthy subsidiary inquiry then asks whether, even supposing (per a hypothesis later revealed to be false, since Article 2 established that the angel does cross the medium) the angel does not cross the medium, its motion would still be instantaneous or temporal, working through an intricate dialectic about last/first instants, the impossibility of simultaneous multi-location, the need for intervening instants (and hence intervening time) between any two given instants, and the correspondence problem between the angel's own measure and our continuous time. Giles resolves this by distinguishing time as formally 'number' (only accidentally continuous, when it happens to inhere in continuous celestial motion) from time as bare succession of instants; using this distinction along with the analysis of priority/posteriority and the special status of the angel's transition as not itself the terminus of any prior motion (unlike ordinary corporeal mutations, which always terminate a preceding motion), he shows that a succession of two adjacent instants, without intervening time, can still count as 'time' in the relevant sense, so that angelic motion, even without medium-crossing, would be temporal rather than instantaneous. The article separately resolves an analogous subsidiary question about the soul's departure from the body at death: because such departure is the terminus of the body's corruption (an actual motion), it follows the ordinary whole-time/boundary-instant pattern and is properly instantaneous relative to the corruption it terminates — unless the soul, though ceasing to be the body's substantial form, continues to be present in the body as a mover or via application of virtue, in which case its departure follows the angel-like discontinuous-time pattern instead and is not necessarily instantaneous. Extensive determinatio material also engages the medieval physical debate (via Avempace and the Commentator/Averroes) over whether time in motion is caused by resistance of the medium or by distance of termini, concluding that time is required wherever there is some resistance — broadly construed to include the mere actual distinctness of mover from moved or of an applying virtue from its object — which suffices to explain time in angelic, animal, and celestial motion alike, without appeal to medial resistance.
claims: Angelic motion is always in time, whether achieved by application of virtue to diverse spaces or in an assumed body.

The time proper to an angel's motion by application of virtue is a discontinuous succession of (at minimum two) instants, differing in kind from the continuous time that measures celestial motion, yet still properly called time, since time is formally a number and only accidentally continuous.

Time in motion, generally, is required wherever there is resistance between mover and moved, broadly construed to include the mere actual distinctness of mover and moved (or of an applying virtue and its object), not resistance of the medium alone.

The soul's departure from the body at death is, in the ordinary case, instantaneous (as the terminus of bodily corruption), but can instead follow the angel-like discontinuous pattern (and thus need not be strictly instantaneous) if the soul remains present in the body as mover or by application of virtue after ceasing to be its substantial form.
concepts: time as number vs. time as continuum
discrete/discontinuous time (succession of instants without intervening time)
soul's presence by application of virtue after ceasing to be form

Gi9qrR-f83308.summary: This quaestio treats the motion of angels across three articles. Article 1 establishes that motion belongs to angels not merely metaphorically (as a figure for their operation, following Dionysius's threefold rectilinear/circular/oblique pattern shared with God and soul) but in a qualified proper sense, grounded in the succession of their immanent and transitive operations rather than in any change of essence or power — angelic motion being called equivocally 'motion' relative to bodily motion, though analogically like alteration and local motion. Article 2 argues that, despite the angel's nature not absolutely requiring place, an angel as part of the ordered, interconnected universe cannot pass from one place to another without traversing (by application of virtue, not commensuration) the intervening medium. Article 3, the most technically elaborate, establishes that angelic motion is always measured by time — whether the angel moves in an assumed body or by application of virtue to successive spaces — and works out, against Aristotle's authority (which concerns only bodily motion) and via the Avempace/Commentator debate on the cause of time in motion (medial resistance vs. distance of termini, resolved by Giles as resistance broadly construed), a doctrine of a properly angelic, discontinuous kind of time (bare succession of instants, as opposed to the continuum that is the passio of celestial motion) sufficient to preserve the per se temporality of all genuine motion. A parallel subsidiary treatment of the soul's departure from the body at death shows that this transition is ordinarily instantaneous (as the terminus of bodily corruption) but can instead follow the angelic, non-instantaneous pattern if the soul remains present in the body (as mover, or by application of virtue) after ceasing to be its substantial form. Across all three articles, the governing strategy is to find, between the pure immateriality of God and the full materiality of bodies, a qualified, analogically extended sense in which motion, place, medium-crossing, and time can be attributed to angels.
claims: Motion, in a qualified but genuine sense, belongs to angels, grounded in succession among their operations rather than in change of essence.
An angel, as part of the ordered universe, cannot pass between places without traversing the intervening medium by application of virtue.

Angelic motion, whether in an assumed body or by application of virtue, is always measured by time, though this time can be a discontinuous succession of instants distinct in kind from the continuous time measuring celestial motion.
The soul's departure from the body at death is ordinarily instantaneous, but can instead be non-instantaneous if the soul remains present in the body after ceasing to be its substantial form.
concepts: presence by operation vs. by commensuration
discontinuous ('angelic') time vs. continuous celestial time
resistance broadly construed as cause of time in motion
analogical extension of physical concepts (motion, place, time) to separate substances
